reason: Both arms denote the same security mechanism of restricting who may reach a resource — maturity spans treat it as the thing an organisation operates ("How does your organization manage access control to AI systems and datasets?" / "access controls for training sets or production data") while SLSA treats it as a baseline control on artifacts ("Access control is still important, but SLSA goes further to provide defense in depth"), which is one concept viewed from the governance and the supply-chain angle rather than two things sharing a label.

The publication-actionability span fixes a clear sense — "A list of single or combined access modes that are sufficient to understand all the intellectual content of a resource" (perceptual/consumption modality) — but the organisational-maturity span contains no access-mode phrase at all, only inventory contents such as "Special rights and considerations for intellectual property, licensed works, or personal, privileged, proprietary or sensitive data", which suggests but does not verbatim establish a permissions/access-control sense, so there is no grounded basis to split.

Both evidenced arms denote obtainability of the data itself — publication actionability: "Accessibility relates to the ease with which data users can obtain an agency's", training-data readiness: "The dataset's accessibility requires a platform with controlled access, considering privacy or licensing constraints" — two angles (dissemination ease vs. gated access) on one concept, while the organisational-maturity arm has no span and so cannot support a split.

Both arms use accountability as the normative principle of answerability for an AI system's conduct rather than a property of a data artifact — maturity: "Trustworthy AI depends upon accountability. Accountability presupposes transparency" alongside "Key Practices to Help Ensure Accountability in Federal Use of AI"; publication: "It is important to make sure that the same accountability exists for AI assistants," which explicitly imports the same answerability standard onto AI systems rather than describing a file-level attribute.

Every arm invokes the same closeness-to-truth measurement, only applied to different bearers — maturity: "Accuracy measures whether a model's prediction matches ground truth"; publication: "Accuracy refers to the closeness of the administrative record data values to their"; training-data: "Accuracy is directly threatened by T2 (False State Injection)" — and the one real polysemy (model-output accuracy vs. data-value accuracy) runs *within* the maturity arm ("data integrity and accuracy") and *within* the publication arm ("accuracy and relevancy of LLM responses"), so it is cross-cutting and licenses no arm-aligned split.

Both arms use the term for the same practice of deliberately probing a system to induce failure — maturity arm: "adversarial testing of AI systems under stress conditions to seek out failure modes or vulnerabilities", publication arm (in negation): "this is not adversarial testing – questions were not selected to try to force the assistants into mistakes" — the second is the same concept described from the evaluator's side, not a different referent.

Neither arm supplies a quotable span — both grounding strings are the bare term "Agency Head" — but both nodes come from US federal executive-branch instruments ("Executive Order 14319: Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government" and "M-19-23: Phase 1 Implementation of the Evidence Act") in which "Agency Head" is the same fixed role designation (the head of a federal agency), a person-role that does not change referent with the construct arm, so there is no evidence of, and no plausible mechanism for, a split.

Both arms refer to the same ontological kind — an autonomous AI software consumer/actor — with the maturity arm framing it as a deployment target ("plan to develop or deploy AI agents") and the actionability arm framing the identical entity as the data consumer ("AI agents require clean, structured, and unambiguous data to perform tasks accurately" / "increased access to and use of official data and statistics by AI agents"), which is one concept seen from the builder's and the consumer's angle rather than two things wearing one word.

Both spans treat "AI ecosystem" as the same broad aggregate of AI actors, technologies and institutions viewed from two angles — competitive scale in the maturity arm ("Whoever has the largest AI ecosystem will set global AI standards") and custodial responsibility over that same aggregate in the actionability arm ("an active stewardship role over the AI ecosystem itself") — with neither span narrowing it to an organisational capability or a data-product property.

Both arms use the term for the same underlying thing — human capacity to understand and work with AI — differing only in which population is being built up: the maturity arm's "Make AI literacy a core competency" / "most employees will need 'AI literacy'" targets the workforce, while the actionability arm's "committed to ongoing AI literacy to support citizens" and "Many of us are passionate about AI literacy, and have invested time and effort into pilot projects" targets the public, which is an audience variation on one concept rather than the type shift (human capability vs. file property) that would justify a split.

The organisational-maturity arm predicates the label of a person — "When does a user become “AI-ready”?" — a state of human competence/calibration, whereas both other arms predicate it of a data artifact, "data should be “AI-Ready”" (publication actionability) and "a framework for data publishers to make their datasets AI-ready" (training-data readiness), so the seed sense driving the current scope note is a human-readiness concept wearing the same word as a dataset property.
